Renal Roulette

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Is the public health care rationing, of South Africans in dire need of dialysis, a death sentence for patients with chronic kidney disease?

Unique Selling Point:
Unlike in the private medical sector where dialysis is mostly available for patients suffering from chronic kidney disease, within the public sector the only way to get dialysis treatment is if you are eligible for a kidney transplant. If you are not eligible for a kidney transplant you will never get on the State dialysis programme. Many people who may not be eligible for transplant can live long and productive lives on dialysis. If these people do not receive dialysis the probability of them dying soon is high. But for patients who are eligible for transplant and are on the state’s list for dialysis, they may never get to the point of transplant or dialysis because the waiting list is too long, and they too may die soon. The reason for this is there are not enough organ donors to help the queues move faster. Moreover, even if you have a willing compatible donor you cannot skip the queue in terms of receiving much needed dialysis. So the probability that you may die soon is also high.
People in need of dialysis but not necessarily a kidney transplant would however require this treatment for the rest of their lives, and at the cost of R 200 000 per patient per year, is it just too much of an ask of the already stretched public healthcare funds.

Summary:
The South African Health care system is bleeding dry when it comes to funding across the board, and never more so when it comes to patients who suffer from chronic kidney disease. For the most part the State is unable to provide adequate care for anyone needing dialysis treatment unless they are eligible for a kidney transplant, and even if they qualify, they may never get there and die in the process of waiting. The reasons for this are that each province has limited slots for dialysis, for example at Charlotte Maxeke, there are only 150 slots for Dialysis and the waiting list is over a thousand, but there may only be 40 kidneys available for transplant at any time.

Further information:
Clinically speaking, many patients, including those with co-morbidity issues like diabetes, obesity, and even heart disease, would have a prolonged and better quality of life with dialysis treatment, but without it, they will die much sooner. However, the South African state employs strict rationing in deciding who can get this treatment, because at R 200 000 per patient per year the cost is prohibitive to being universally available.
The Barbara Hogan guidelines that clinicians use to choose who gets on the queue for dialysis are strict but do not seem to be applied equally across provinces.

In Kwazulu-Natal we have two case studies who initially did qualify for dialysis, but the one got too ill to qualify for transplant so lost eligibility for dialysis - the other, on strict adherence to the guidelines, should not have qualified, but somehow managed to get on the programme, but then was removed from the programme, because they couldn’t treat him anymore. Both of these patients are now being treated at a Renal clinic in Durban that was set up by an NGO in reaction to the limited access to state dialysis treatment. We interview Dr Mohamed Solwa of the IMA-IQRAA Renal Dialysis Project and the two case studies – a 56 yr old woman and a 28 yr old man. Mrs Bagus lives on The Bluff – lost her job because of kidney illness – was on state dialysis for a year then got taken off the programme – basically left to die. Now she is getting dialysis at Dr Solwa’s IMA-IQRAA Renal Dialysis Project, and is back on her feet and looking for a job. So even though she is not eligible for transplant due to a blockage in her throat artery, she is able to function well on dialysis treatment. She says that the State hospital had left her to die.

The way the NGO’s generally work, is that they fund the patient for a year, while they get them onto a medical aid, and then the medical aid takes over the funding the patient for dialysis.

At 28 Lungelo Hadebe, has suffered from obesity and diabetes from an early age. According to the National guidelines, merely by the fact that he is morbidly obese and a diabetic, he would not be eligible for a transplant and therefore not eligible for dialysis, but because the guidelines are not necessarily applied the same in each province, he was lucky enough to get onto dialysis in a state hospital in Petermaritzburg for a while, but then the treatment stopped and he was asked to leave the programme, basically again left to die. He managed to get help from the same Ngo, and is currently managing to work and study law at the same time.

Around the country, long waiting lists bare witness to heart wrenching stories like that of Chanté Domitreme. She entered the dialysis programme and she did have a willing donor, her boyfriend, whose kidney proved to be a blood match. But while Chanté was in the queue waiting for dialysis she got very ill and needed dialysis but couldn’t get it. Sadly she deteriorated even further and the palliative care was inadequate. Now she is much too sick for a transplant. Initially, if she could have skipped the queue because her boyfriend volunteered his kidney for her, who knows what her story might have been. But queue jumping under any circumstance is not allowed in the public healthcare system as it is considered unconstitutional.

Prof. Graham Paget: Head of SA Renal Society speaks to the state approach and how dire the situation is. But that this kind of rationing is the only way the state can cope with available resources, but believes that more could be done even now. More units and definitely, more donors.

Dr Waddee, who has a private practice in Donny Gordon Hospital JHB, believes the state should
be doing more and as for the palliative care in state hospitals of patients who cannot get dialysis, of whom he sees about two every week, he says “They don’t care, they’ll just send you home to die.” He says the situation is dire and that the public health sector is not doing enough for end state kidney patients. He speaks directly to the fact that many patients that come to him, who have been rejected by the public sector, can live very well on dialysis. When he can he refers patients to various NGO’s but there again the queues are getting longer.

Prof Alex Van Den Heever, Health economist, speaks to the analysis of the state’s rationing of health treatments. Where do we draw the line and what is the price of life?

Questions to the Department of Health will include:
Guidelines are applied differently in different provinces, why?
What if anything is being done by the Department to improve access for patients?
Our understanding is that waiting lists are so long that patients die in the process of waiting. Additionally, clarity on if a patient has an available volunteer kidney donor, why are they unable to be processed ahead of other patients?

We confront the Department of Health as to why it is unconstitutional for someone to come with a donor and get fast-tracked for transplant, even if it would save waiting times on dialysis machines.
Prof Graham Paget who practices at Wits Donald Gordon Medical Centre, said they did try using the system of people with donors to get ahead of the queue, a few years ago, but were told by the Department of Health to desist immediately, basically the Department says that it goes against Human Rights, in that, the consequences of ‘accident of birth’ events should not be rewarded by favouritism. Even so, the argument may never be straightforward because of the lack of funding to make the situation less acute.

So we ask the department if this really is the best way to save the most peoples’ lives and what could the department be doing to improve this dire state of affairs. After all, a country like Thailand, with similar GDP per capita to South Africa, managed to treat 1515 per million of its population with renal replacement therapy in 2017 as compared to only 190 per million population in South Africa [United States Renal Data System 2018 Annual Data Report].

Is this crisis all about the targeting of healthcare funding, the sum of healthcare funding or inefficiencies in distributing funds? ... or a combination of all three?
In terms of rationing there is also the complication of who is it more important to save? A young individual with no dependents who the treatment could buy many years of quality life, or an older breadwinner who by saving, one would be enabling the support of their dependent family members to healthier future lives.



CASE STUDIES:

Chanté Domitrenne: Initially she got on the dialysis list and her boyfriend's kidney was found to be a match and he offered it for transplant. However, in the meantime Chanté got sicker such that she didn't get on dialysis and now she is too sick for a transplant.

Mrs Bagus: Age 56, lives on The Bluff – lost her job because of kidney illness – was on state dialysis for a year then got taken off the programme – basically left to die. Now she is getting dialysis at Dr Solwa’s IMA-IQRAA Renal Dialysis Project.

Lungelo Hadebe: Age 28, obese diabetic who was on state dialysis but then taken off it. He has approached Dr Solwa’s IMA-IQRAA Renal Dialysis Project.


EXPERTS:

Prof. Graham Paget: Head of SA Renal Society
Charlotte Maxeke Hospital
- Speaks to the state approach and how dire the situation is

Dr Waddee – Private practice in Donny Gordon Hospital JHB, believes the state should be doing more and as for the palliative care in state hospitals of patients who cannot get dialysis, he says “They don’t care, they’ll just send you home to die.”

Dr Mohamed Solwa of the Durban NGO (IMA-IQRAA Renal Dialysis Project) speaks to his organizations approach to the crisis and their methodology to try to ease the situation and save lives.

Ms MP Matsoso: DG National Department of Health, Dept of Health.

Prof Alex Van Den Heever, Health economist – speaks to the analysis of the state’s rationing of health treatments.

Press Release:


What is the price of a life? We investigate the rationing of state health care as thousands of South Africans with end stage kidney disease are refused life-saving dialysis. Faced with kidney failure and in desperate need of an organ transplant, why do patients with willing donors, still remain on the transplant waiting list in the public healthcare system?


Script:


Link: This is the renal unit at the Charlotte Maxeke hospital in Johannesburg where patients suffering from end-stage kidney disease are treated. They're currently receiving dialysis which is basically an artificial kidney. They spend an average of 4 hours per session three times a week. Without this machine they would die.

Siyavuya: I have been waiting for a transplant for 15 years.

VO: Because 43 year old Siyavuya Zozo has a rare blood type he has spent those 15 years on dialysis waiting for a suitable kidney.

Siyavuya: I'm an architect by profession and I have a family who actually rely on me for support.

VO: He suffers from end stage kidney disease and has been treated in the public health care sector for the last 12 years.

Siyavuya: When I started, I started in private, I then had to scale down and that meant no medical aid, just go to the public hospital and get yourself treatment.

VO: It costs the state around 200 000 rand a year to treat one patient on dialysis.

Link: But with limited slots around the country, constrained funds, the waiting list for treatment is very long and some patients will never get to see the inside of a ward like this.

Paget: The sad fact is that certainly in our hospital, the average time till your turn comes is around 18 months.

VO: Professor Graham Paget, head of nephrology at the Charlotte Maxeke Hospital in Gauteng, explains that the waiting time for a kidney transplant is around 7 to 8 years, during which time people need dialysis, so the limited slots are not vacated quickly enough.

Paget: So we have about an 80% mortality on that waiting list. It's called a waiting list but if you really need dialysis, well you don't survive, it's one of those things.

VO: In 2009 guidelines were set by then Minister of Health Barbara Hogan as to who qualifies for dialysis. The main criterion is that a patient is eligible for a kidney transplant. If a patient has co-morbidities like obesity or cancer they will not qualify.

Paget: So if you were deemed to be not able to get a transplant then you would have to self fund. Unfortunately the costs are prohibitive for the vast majority of South Africans.

VO: Siyavuya considers himself lucky to be on the state programme.

Siyavuya: Seeing other people who can't be accepted onto the program, it actually pains me because you know it means that you are going to go home and die .

Link: So you'd imagine that if you have end stage kidney disease and you have a matching donor, this should be a good enough reason to get ahead in the queue. Apparently, and according to the national guidelines, it doesn't work that way.

VO: Chanté Domitremé has spent her life rescuing animals through her Bunny Sanctuary in Centurion. But now her own life is in danger - from the effects of polycystic kidney disease.

Jonathan: I know her to be a very independent, very strong woman and this disease has just taken her down so quickly and so fast. And I think if it wasn't for the animals, she wouldn't be fighting right now.

VO: Three years ago she had a willing and initially matching kidney donor in her long time friend and business partner Jonathan Steyn, and was put on the hemodialysis waiting list at Helen Joseph Hospital, in Gauteng.

Jonathan: She was number 25 on the list and being 25 on the list could mean anything from two years to five years we were hoping that there would be some criteria because I'm a live donor that she would be moved up on the hemodialysis list and they said that that does not happen.

Mac: If someone had a willing donor, are they able to skip the queue?
Paget: You can't skip the queue. The only way it'll work is if you have enough time with your own kidney to allow the work up to proceed along the legislative lines. When we look at donors, we look at how many of them through medical, psychological and social workup actually make it to that point, we turn down 70% of those donors.

Jonathan: The state couldn't help, she was put on a list but you wait for years and she does not have years.

VO: In 1997 the Constitutional Court vindicated rationing of dialysis in the Soobramoney case judgement, ruling that the rights to life and health care are dependent on the State's available resources.

Pillay: Unfortunately we cannot provide all services that are needed to everyone.
VO: According to Dr Yogan Pillay, Deputy Director General of the Department of Health, because dialysis is so expensive, the line is drawn at transplant eligibility.

Pillay: It is rather an unfortunate situation and our solution to that is to get the resources from the public and the private sectors, put them into one pool and make all of the resources equitably available to every citizen. But even in that instance we will not have all the money to provide every service to everyone.

VO: Economist, Professor Alex Van den Heever, is critical of the way funds are allocated in the public health sector and believes the value placed on a life is far more complex.

Alex: You've got to look at the value of somebody to their family, their entire context, you can't look at it as a crude number crunching exercise. What you have to do is exercise enormous care when somebody is basically being sent home to die.

VO: Excluded from the transplant programme due to medical complications, and unable to afford private medical fees, Chanté's health has deteriorated, with only short spurts of palliative care through state hospitals.

Jonathan: If she received dialysis three years ago she would have been able to lead a fairly normal life.

VO: Dr Shoyab Wadee is a nephrologist in private practice. He sees around 2 patients a week who have failed to get on the State's dialysis programme.

Wadee: Professor Moosa from Cape Town did a study a couple of years back looking at the number of patients turned down in their system and extrapolating them across SA and he estimated that we're sending home one jumbo jet filled with people every month to die in SA.
Mac: That's about 400 people
Wadee: Based on the registry, ja. Based on the registry we estimate that we should have between 40 and 60 thousand patients on dialysis in SA. but we have about 10 000, so those other 40 000 are people that have already died, they should have been living on dialysis.

Mac: There are many patients who suffer from comorbidities like diabetes, heart disease or even obesity, will not qualify for a kidney transplant but they're able to live a normal, productive, lives on dialysis treatment.

Roslyn: I go for dialysis 3 times a week and that's for 4 hours, so my day starts at about 10:30 and I come home at about 4:30

VO: Like Chanté, 57 year old Roslyn Bagus also suffers from polycystic kidney disease but has been on dialysis since 2017.

Roslyn: It is a long tiring day, so I call it my job.

VO: For Roslyn the road to staying alive hasn't been easy. In 2017 she fell very ill and was admitted to the Albert Lithuli state hospital in Durban.

Roslyn: They gave me dialysis immediately which helped a whole lot.

VO: But in July 2018 she was called in for a meeting with the doctor and told to bring a witness.

Roselyn: And he said to me that I'm taken off the program which was a great shock for me because without dialysis, you're dead.

VO: Roselyn's neck arteries were blocked, so she was no longer eligible for transplant .


Roslyn: So I went to Greys hospital and when i got there, there was absolutely no place and the sister in charge of the dialysis unit gave me IMA's number

VO: IMA,The Islamic Medical Association, is one of a few charitable, non profit organisations that has funded dialysis treatment nationally for the last 15 years, through partnerships with private business, banks, and community engagement. Dr Mahomed Solwa coordinates their renal unit in Durban.

Solwa: A lot of them come here not knowing where to turn to. and they'll give you their stories to how the state didn't put them on the program and we accepted them and today they are leading very meaningful lives.

VO: IMA funds patients, with the aim of getting them onto medical aid, which then covers them for dialysis treatment under prescribed minimum benefits. IMA supplements the payments thereafter.

Lungelo: I was diagnosed at Grey's Hospital in Pietermaritzburg for nephrotic syndrome and then it was later confirmed to be chronic kidney disease.

VO: 28 year old activist and law student, Lungelo Hadebe, a diabetic since the age of seven, was also given a lifeline through IMA when he was taken off State dialysis.

Lungelo: They told me that they are taking me out of dialysis end of the month.
Mac: What was their reasoning for that?
Lungelo: They said I'm no longer a candidate for transplantation. They said my heart is not strong.
Mac: Did you feel that you had been condemned to a death sentence?
Lungelo: Yes, it's very clear. I understand what dialysis meant to me, and if I can no longer get that quality of life, I'm dead.

Solwa: Once you have a condition, if you're diagnosed with diabetes, you're diagnosed with hypertension you certainly cannot turn away patients, it's a human rights issue.

Mac: And how has it been since you were here?
Lungelo: It has made me to be able to dare to dream again, I'm good. I even took a decision to go back and study.

VO: Critics of the State guidelines for chronic renal dialysis argue that a progressive realisation of rights is not being implemented, particularly since South Africa has a poor donor culture.

Alex: It looks like an arbitrary exclusion because there is no proper transplant program that is being developed in order to expand access to dialysis. Whereas the progressive realisation aspect requires an active stance of the government to change what's available to people and deepen it consistently over time.

Mac: So simply put there is a shortage of dialysis in SA?
Paget: Absolutely so if we compare ourselves to countries with similar GDP, the private service in the country is more or less keeping pace with that whereas the state is quite far behind.
Mac: And what are those international best practices?
Paget: Ja, so looking at about 800 persons per million which is funny enough what the private sector runs at and we're running at 80 per million population. Sadly in terms of transplant we're way down, we're 3 or 4 per million so we need to do a lot better.

Mac: A lot of people are getting turned away,for various reasons, one of them being the fact that they don't qualify for a transplant. We're sentencing them to death.
Pillay: Well unfortunately we have to focus on prevention. Now we have a process in place to revise the guideline including how to license both private and public units that provide dialysis under what conditions they will be provided et et cetera and part of it would be also to look at the guidelines in terms of eligibility.

VO: This process still has to go through parliament and for public comment. In the meantime people like Chanté have little hope for survival.

Jonathan: Her kidney function is below 10 percent . She's bleeding from her kidneys. She suffers from extreme pain, fatigue. She needs help with simple tasks. So she has really at this stage no quality of life and she's deemed as terminal.

Drew_Milligan TRL_0080 TX Details Back references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 08 March 2020 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 01 April 2020 Press Release: What is the price of a life? We investigate the rationing of state health care as thousands of South Africans with end stage kidney disease are refused life-saving dialysis. Faced with kidney failure and in desperate need of an organ transplant, why do patients with willing donors, still remain on the transplant waiting list in the public healthcare system? Script: Link: This is the renal unit at the Charlotte Maxeke hospital in Johannesburg where patients suffering from end-stage kidney disease are treated. They're currently receiving dialysis which is basically an artificial kidney. They spend an average of 4 hours per session three times a week. Without this machine they would die. Siyavuya: I have been waiting for a transplant for 15 years. VO: Because 43 year old Siyavuya Zozo has a rare blood type he has spent those 15 years on dialysis waiting for a suitable kidney. Siyavuya: I'm an architect by profession and I have a family who actually rely on me for support. VO: He suffers from end stage kidney disease and has been treated in the public health care sector for the last 12 years. Siyavuya: When I started, I started in private, I then had to scale down and that meant no medical aid, just go to the public hospital and get yourself treatment. VO: It costs the state around 200 000 rand a year to treat one patient on dialysis. Link: But with limited slots around the country, constrained funds, the waiting list for treatment is very long and some patients will never get to see the inside of a ward like this. Paget: The sad fact is that certainly in our hospital, the average time till your turn comes is around 18 months. VO: Professor Graham Paget, head of nephrology at the Charlotte Maxeke Hospital in Gauteng, explains that the waiting time for a kidney transplant is around 7 to 8 years, during which time people need dialysis, so the limited slots are not vacated quickly enough. Paget: So we have about an 80% mortality on that waiting list. It's called a waiting list but if you really need dialysis, well you don't survive, it's one of those things. VO: In 2009 guidelines were set by then Minister of Health Barbara Hogan as to who qualifies for dialysis. The main criterion is that a patient is eligible for a kidney transplant. If a patient has co-morbidities like obesity or cancer they will not qualify. Paget: So if you were deemed to be not able to get a transplant then you would have to self fund. Unfortunately the costs are prohibitive for the vast majority of South Africans. VO: Siyavuya considers himself lucky to be on the state programme. Siyavuya: Seeing other people who can't be accepted onto the program, it actually pains me because you know it means that you are going to go home and die . Link: So you'd imagine that if you have end stage kidney disease and you have a matching donor, this should be a good enough reason to get ahead in the queue. Apparently, and according to the national guidelines, it doesn't work that way. VO: Chanté Domitremé has spent her life rescuing animals through her Bunny Sanctuary in Centurion. But now her own life is in danger - from the effects of polycystic kidney disease. Jonathan: I know her to be a very independent, very strong woman and this disease has just taken her down so quickly and so fast. And I think if it wasn't for the animals, she wouldn't be fighting right now. VO: Three years ago she had a willing and initially matching kidney donor in her long time friend and business partner Jonathan Steyn, and was put on the hemodialysis waiting list at Helen Joseph Hospital, in Gauteng. Jonathan: She was number 25 on the list and being 25 on the list could mean anything from two years to five years we were hoping that there would be some criteria because I'm a live donor that she would be moved up on the hemodialysis list and they said that that does not happen. Mac: If someone had a willing donor, are they able to skip the queue? Paget: You can't skip the queue. The only way it'll work is if you have enough time with your own kidney to allow the work up to proceed along the legislative lines. When we look at donors, we look at how many of them through medical, psychological and social workup actually make it to that point, we turn down 70% of those donors. Jonathan: The state couldn't help, she was put on a list but you wait for years and she does not have years. VO: In 1997 the Constitutional Court vindicated rationing of dialysis in the Soobramoney case judgement, ruling that the rights to life and health care are dependent on the State's available resources. Pillay: Unfortunately we cannot provide all services that are needed to everyone. VO: According to Dr Yogan Pillay, Deputy Director General of the Department of Health, because dialysis is so expensive, the line is drawn at transplant eligibility. Pillay: It is rather an unfortunate situation and our solution to that is to get the resources from the public and the private sectors, put them into one pool and make all of the resources equitably available to every citizen. But even in that instance we will not have all the money to provide every service to everyone. VO: Economist, Professor Alex Van den Heever, is critical of the way funds are allocated in the public health sector and believes the value placed on a life is far more complex. Alex: You've got to look at the value of somebody to their family, their entire context, you can't look at it as a crude number crunching exercise. What you have to do is exercise enormous care when somebody is basically being sent home to die. VO: Excluded from the transplant programme due to medical complications, and unable to afford private medical fees, Chanté's health has deteriorated, with only short spurts of palliative care through state hospitals. Jonathan: If she received dialysis three years ago she would have been able to lead a fairly normal life. VO: Dr Shoyab Wadee is a nephrologist in private practice. He sees around 2 patients a week who have failed to get on the State's dialysis programme. Wadee: Professor Moosa from Cape Town did a study a couple of years back looking at the number of patients turned down in their system and extrapolating them across SA and he estimated that we're sending home one jumbo jet filled with people every month to die in SA. Mac: That's about 400 people Wadee: Based on the registry, ja. Based on the registry we estimate that we should have between 40 and 60 thousand patients on dialysis in SA. but we have about 10 000, so those other 40 000 are people that have already died, they should have been living on dialysis. Mac: There are many patients who suffer from comorbidities like diabetes, heart disease or even obesity, will not qualify for a kidney transplant but they're able to live a normal, productive, lives on dialysis treatment. Roslyn: I go for dialysis 3 times a week and that's for 4 hours, so my day starts at about 10:30 and I come home at about 4:30 VO: Like Chanté, 57 year old Roslyn Bagus also suffers from polycystic kidney disease but has been on dialysis since 2017. Roslyn: It is a long tiring day, so I call it my job. VO: For Roslyn the road to staying alive hasn't been easy. In 2017 she fell very ill and was admitted to the Albert Lithuli state hospital in Durban. Roslyn: They gave me dialysis immediately which helped a whole lot. VO: But in July 2018 she was called in for a meeting with the doctor and told to bring a witness. Roselyn: And he said to me that I'm taken off the program which was a great shock for me because without dialysis, you're dead. VO: Roselyn's neck arteries were blocked, so she was no longer eligible for transplant . Roslyn: So I went to Greys hospital and when i got there, there was absolutely no place and the sister in charge of the dialysis unit gave me IMA's number VO: IMA,The Islamic Medical Association, is one of a few charitable, non profit organisations that has funded dialysis treatment nationally for the last 15 years, through partnerships with private business, banks, and community engagement. Dr Mahomed Solwa coordinates their renal unit in Durban. Solwa: A lot of them come here not knowing where to turn to. and they'll give you their stories to how the state didn't put them on the program and we accepted them and today they are leading very meaningful lives. VO: IMA funds patients, with the aim of getting them onto medical aid, which then covers them for dialysis treatment under prescribed minimum benefits. IMA supplements the payments thereafter. Lungelo: I was diagnosed at Grey's Hospital in Pietermaritzburg for nephrotic syndrome and then it was later confirmed to be chronic kidney disease. VO: 28 year old activist and law student, Lungelo Hadebe, a diabetic since the age of seven, was also given a lifeline through IMA when he was taken off State dialysis. Lungelo: They told me that they are taking me out of dialysis end of the month. Mac: What was their reasoning for that? Lungelo: They said I'm no longer a candidate for transplantation. They said my heart is not strong. Mac: Did you feel that you had been condemned to a death sentence? Lungelo: Yes, it's very clear. I understand what dialysis meant to me, and if I can no longer get that quality of life, I'm dead. Solwa: Once you have a condition, if you're diagnosed with diabetes, you're diagnosed with hypertension you certainly cannot turn away patients, it's a human rights issue. Mac: And how has it been since you were here? Lungelo: It has made me to be able to dare to dream again, I'm good. I even took a decision to go back and study. VO: Critics of the State guidelines for chronic renal dialysis argue that a progressive realisation of rights is not being implemented, particularly since South Africa has a poor donor culture. Alex: It looks like an arbitrary exclusion because there is no proper transplant program that is being developed in order to expand access to dialysis. Whereas the progressive realisation aspect requires an active stance of the government to change what's available to people and deepen it consistently over time. Mac: So simply put there is a shortage of dialysis in SA? Paget: Absolutely so if we compare ourselves to countries with similar GDP, the private service in the country is more or less keeping pace with that whereas the state is quite far behind. Mac: And what are those international best practices? Paget: Ja, so looking at about 800 persons per million which is funny enough what the private sector runs at and we're running at 80 per million population. Sadly in terms of transplant we're way down, we're 3 or 4 per million so we need to do a lot better. Mac: A lot of people are getting turned away,for various reasons, one of them being the fact that they don't qualify for a transplant. We're sentencing them to death. Pillay: Well unfortunately we have to focus on prevention. Now we have a process in place to revise the guideline including how to license both private and public units that provide dialysis under what conditions they will be provided et et cetera and part of it would be also to look at the guidelines in terms of eligibility. VO: This process still has to go through parliament and for public comment. In the meantime people like Chanté have little hope for survival. Jonathan: Her kidney function is below 10 percent . She's bleeding from her kidneys. She suffers from extreme pain, fatigue. She needs help with simple tasks. So she has really at this stage no quality of life and she's deemed as terminal.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Is the public health care rationing, of South Africans in dire need of dialysis, a death sentence for patients with chronic kidney disease?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Unlike in the private medical sector where dialysis is mostly available for patients suffering from chronic kidney disease, within the public sector the only way to get dialysis treatment is if you are eligible for a kidney transplant. If you are not eligible for a kidney transplant you will never get on the State dialysis programme. Many people who may not be eligible for transplant can live long and productive lives on dialysis. If these people do not receive dialysis the probability of them dying soon is high. But for patients who are eligible for transplant and are on the state’s list for dialysis, they may never get to the point of transplant or dialysis because the waiting list is too long, and they too may die soon. The reason for this is there are not enough organ donors to help the queues move faster. Moreover, even if you have a willing compatible donor you cannot skip the queue in terms of receiving much needed dialysis. So the probability that you may die soon is also high. People in need of dialysis but not necessarily a kidney transplant would however require this treatment for the rest of their lives, and at the cost of R 200 000 per patient per year, is it just too much of an ask of the already stretched public healthcare funds.
metadata.Summary: The South African Health care system is bleeding dry when it comes to funding across the board, and never more so when it comes to patients who suffer from chronic kidney disease. For the most part the State is unable to provide adequate care for anyone needing dialysis treatment unless they are eligible for a kidney transplant, and even if they qualify, they may never get there and die in the process of waiting. The reasons for this are that each province has limited slots for dialysis, for example at Charlotte Maxeke, there are only 150 slots for Dialysis and the waiting list is over a thousand, but there may only be 40 kidneys available for transplant at any time.
metadata.Further information: Clinically speaking, many patients, including those with co-morbidity issues like diabetes, obesity, and even heart disease, would have a prolonged and better quality of life with dialysis treatment, but without it, they will die much sooner. However, the South African state employs strict rationing in deciding who can get this treatment, because at R 200 000 per patient per year the cost is prohibitive to being universally available. The Barbara Hogan guidelines that clinicians use to choose who gets on the queue for dialysis are strict but do not seem to be applied equally across provinces. In Kwazulu-Natal we have two case studies who initially did qualify for dialysis, but the one got too ill to qualify for transplant so lost eligibility for dialysis - the other, on strict adherence to the guidelines, should not have qualified, but somehow managed to get on the programme, but then was removed from the programme, because they couldn’t treat him anymore. Both of these patients are now being treated at a Renal clinic in Durban that was set up by an NGO in reaction to the limited access to state dialysis treatment. We interview Dr Mohamed Solwa of the IMA-IQRAA Renal Dialysis Project and the two case studies – a 56 yr old woman and a 28 yr old man. Mrs Bagus lives on The Bluff – lost her job because of kidney illness – was on state dialysis for a year then got taken off the programme – basically left to die. Now she is getting dialysis at Dr Solwa’s IMA-IQRAA Renal Dialysis Project, and is back on her feet and looking for a job. So even though she is not eligible for transplant due to a blockage in her throat artery, she is able to function well on dialysis treatment. She says that the State hospital had left her to die. The way the NGO’s generally work, is that they fund the patient for a year, while they get them onto a medical aid, and then the medical aid takes over the funding the patient for dialysis. At 28 Lungelo Hadebe, has suffered from obesity and diabetes from an early age. According to the National guidelines, merely by the fact that he is morbidly obese and a diabetic, he would not be eligible for a transplant and therefore not eligible for dialysis, but because the guidelines are not necessarily applied the same in each province, he was lucky enough to get onto dialysis in a state hospital in Petermaritzburg for a while, but then the treatment stopped and he was asked to leave the programme, basically again left to die. He managed to get help from the same Ngo, and is currently managing to work and study law at the same time. Around the country, long waiting lists bare witness to heart wrenching stories like that of Chanté Domitreme. She entered the dialysis programme and she did have a willing donor, her boyfriend, whose kidney proved to be a blood match. But while Chanté was in the queue waiting for dialysis she got very ill and needed dialysis but couldn’t get it. Sadly she deteriorated even further and the palliative care was inadequate. Now she is much too sick for a transplant. Initially, if she could have skipped the queue because her boyfriend volunteered his kidney for her, who knows what her story might have been. But queue jumping under any circumstance is not allowed in the public healthcare system as it is considered unconstitutional. Prof. Graham Paget: Head of SA Renal Society speaks to the state approach and how dire the situation is. But that this kind of rationing is the only way the state can cope with available resources, but believes that more could be done even now. More units and definitely, more donors. Dr Waddee, who has a private practice in Donny Gordon Hospital JHB, believes the state should be doing more and as for the palliative care in state hospitals of patients who cannot get dialysis, of whom he sees about two every week, he says “They don’t care, they’ll just send you home to die.” He says the situation is dire and that the public health sector is not doing enough for end state kidney patients. He speaks directly to the fact that many patients that come to him, who have been rejected by the public sector, can live very well on dialysis. When he can he refers patients to various NGO’s but there again the queues are getting longer. Prof Alex Van Den Heever, Health economist, speaks to the analysis of the state’s rationing of health treatments. Where do we draw the line and what is the price of life? Questions to the Department of Health will include: Guidelines are applied differently in different provinces, why? What if anything is being done by the Department to improve access for patients? Our understanding is that waiting lists are so long that patients die in the process of waiting. Additionally, clarity on if a patient has an available volunteer kidney donor, why are they unable to be processed ahead of other patients? We confront the Department of Health as to why it is unconstitutional for someone to come with a donor and get fast-tracked for transplant, even if it would save waiting times on dialysis machines. Prof Graham Paget who practices at Wits Donald Gordon Medical Centre, said they did try using the system of people with donors to get ahead of the queue, a few years ago, but were told by the Department of Health to desist immediately, basically the Department says that it goes against Human Rights, in that, the consequences of ‘accident of birth’ events should not be rewarded by favouritism. Even so, the argument may never be straightforward because of the lack of funding to make the situation less acute. So we ask the department if this really is the best way to save the most peoples’ lives and what could the department be doing to improve this dire state of affairs. After all, a country like Thailand, with similar GDP per capita to South Africa, managed to treat 1515 per million of its population with renal replacement therapy in 2017 as compared to only 190 per million population in South Africa [United States Renal Data System 2018 Annual Data Report]. Is this crisis all about the targeting of healthcare funding, the sum of healthcare funding or inefficiencies in distributing funds? ... or a combination of all three? In terms of rationing there is also the complication of who is it more important to save? A young individual with no dependents who the treatment could buy many years of quality life, or an older breadwinner who by saving, one would be enabling the support of their dependent family members to healthier future lives. CASE STUDIES: Chanté Domitrenne: Initially she got on the dialysis list and her boyfriend's kidney was found to be a match and he offered it for transplant. However, in the meantime Chanté got sicker such that she didn't get on dialysis and now she is too sick for a transplant. Mrs Bagus: Age 56, lives on The Bluff – lost her job because of kidney illness – was on state dialysis for a year then got taken off the programme – basically left to die. Now she is getting dialysis at Dr Solwa’s IMA-IQRAA Renal Dialysis Project. Lungelo Hadebe: Age 28, obese diabetic who was on state dialysis but then taken off it. He has approached Dr Solwa’s IMA-IQRAA Renal Dialysis Project.
